#seniorhealth  #bloodsugar  #diabetes 
Your feet may reveal important clues about your health. In this video, Healing and Health explores 9 possible foot warning signs associated with diabetes, especially in adults over 50 and seniors. Learn why tingling, numbness, burning sensations, slow-healing sores, swollen feet, unusual skin discoloration, cracked heels, cold feet, and reduced hair growth on the legs deserve attention.

Diabetes can affect circulation and nerves, sometimes causing symptoms in the feet before a person realizes something is wrong. Recognizing changes early and discussing them with a qualified healthcare professional can help you protect your foot health and overall well-being.

Discover practical foot-care habits, the importance of regular checkups, and why blood glucose testing may be necessary when diabetes is suspected. .

Watch until the end to learn how to take better care of your feet as you age.


 Keywords

diabetes warning signs, diabetes symptoms in feet, signs of diabetes in seniors, diabetic foot symptoms, early signs of diabetes, diabetes after 50, diabetes after 60, foot problems in older adults, diabetic neuropathy symptoms, poor circulation in feet, numb feet causes, burning feet at night, swollen feet in seniors, senior health tips, healthy aging

Hashtags

#diabetessymptoms  #diabeteswarning #diabeticfoot  #healthafter50  #healthafter60  #diabetesawareness  #foothealth  #healthyaging  #diabeticneuropathy   #wellnessforseniors  #preventivehealth  

Disclaimer: This video is for educational purposes only and is not a substitute for professional medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment.

Most people believe that diabetes can
only be caught by a blood test. You go
to your doctor, the lab work comes back,
and that's when you find out.
I understand why people think that for
years. That's what most patients told
me, too.
My name is Dr. Michael Carter, and I've
been practicing medicine for over 20
years. And what I've learned, what I see
confirmed in my office every single
week, is that your body starts warning
you about high blood sugar long before
any lab result ever would.
And the very first place your body
speaks up your feet.
The reason I'm making this video today
is because of how many patients I've
seen walk into my office, or worse, walk
into an emergency room, who had every
warning sign for months, sometimes
years, and never knew what they were
looking at.
Today, I'm going to change that for you.
Just last month, I sat down with a
patient, a 67-year-old man, retired,
healthy lifestyle, felt fine.
He came in for a routine checkup.
But before we did any blood work, I
asked him about his feet.
He told me, "My feet have been a little
numb for a while. I figured it was just
age."
He had four of the nine signs I'm going
to show you today.
His fasting blood sugar came back at
214
He was diabetic and had been for over 2
years without knowing it.
So today, I want to show you exactly
what I showed that patient. Nine signs
that were already on his feet and on
millions of feet right now that almost
nobody recognizes for what they are.
For each one, I'll tell you what most
people assume it is, what's actually
happening inside your body, and one
simple daily habit that can protect you.
The American Diabetes Association
estimates that one in five Americans
with diabetes don't even know they have
it. That's over 8 million people walking
around right now with a silent condition
quietly damaging their nerves, their
kidneys, their vision, and yes, their
feet.
The good news, a $12 blood test can
catch this early.
But first, you need to know what to look
for. So, let's get into it.
Sign number one is something almost
every patient has already experienced,
and every single one of them has
explained it away.
Tingling, numbness, that pins and
needles feeling in the feet.
My patients almost always tell me, "Dr.
Parker, my foot just falls asleep
sometimes. I was sitting with my legs
crossed."
And yes, that happens to everyone
occasionally.
But I always ask them, "Is this
happening regularly without a clear
reason?"
Because if the answer is yes, we need to
talk about what's actually going on.
Frequent recurring numbness or tingling
in the feet, what doctors call
peripheral neuropathy, is one of the
earliest signs that blood sugar has been
elevated for some time.
The extra sugar in your bloodstream
begins attacking the outer protective
layer of your nerves.
It's a slow process, which is exactly
why most people miss it.
I use this analogy with my patients all
the time. Think of your nerves like
electrical wires.
Every wire has a plastic coating around
it.
That coating is what allows the signal
to travel cleanly from your brain to
your foot.
When blood sugar stays high, it's like
an acid slowly eating through that
coating.
The wire still works for a while, but
the signals start getting fuzzy.
And that fuzziness,
that's the tingling you feel.
According to the American Diabetes
Association, peripheral neuropathy
affects nearly 50% of people with
diabetes.
It is the single most common
complication, and it almost always
starts in the feet.
Which means right now, tens of millions
of Americans are experiencing this
tingling and writing it off as nothing.
Don't be one of them.
My daily recommendation for every
patient over 60,
a 20 to 30-minute walk every single day.
Not a jog, a walk.
Movement is the best thing you can do to
keep blood flowing to your feet and
protect those nerve endings.
And start reducing added sugar in your
diet today, not next month, today.
Sign number two, and this one my
patients describe as the most
distressing of all because it doesn't
hit them during the day.
It hits them at night when they're alone
and trying to sleep and there is nothing
to distract from it.
A lot of my patients chalk this up to
being on their feet all day
or the summer heat or just fatigue.
And sometimes that's exactly what it is.
But when a patient tells me their feet
feel like they're on fire especially at
night when they're lying down I take
that very seriously.
Burning in the soles of the feet,
particularly at night, is a classic
early sign of diabetic neuropathy.
What's happening is this.
The nerves in your feet have been
damaged by excess sugar

Your brain receives a heat message even

The nerves are misfiring. Think of it

Your feet are at the end of the longest

Cracks appear.

You press your finger into the swollen

#generalanesthesia  #anesthesia  #seniorhealth  #OlderAdults 
What really happens when you undergo general anesthesia after age 60 or 65? In this 22-minute video, Healing and Health explains how anesthesia affects the brain and body, from the initial medications and propofol induction to breathing support, continuous monitoring, waking up, and recovery.

Learn why some older adults may experience temporary confusion, memory difficulties, or changes in concentration after surgery. We explore general versus regional anesthesia, anesthesia awareness, post-operative delirium.

You’ll also discover practical ways to prepare for surgery, questions to ask your anesthesiologist, and why following fasting instructions and discussing all medications and supplements are important.

#diabetes  #bloodsugar  #seniorhealth  #healthyaging 
Are you over 60 and trying to manage your blood sugar? Hydration is an important part of overall health, especially for older adults living with diabetes or prediabetes. In this 24-minute video, Healing and Health explores how dehydration may influence blood glucose levels, why thirst can become less noticeable with age, and how healthy hydration habits fit into diabetes management.

Discover how water supports normal body functions, learn to recognize possible signs of dehydration, and explore practical ways to maintain consistent hydration throughout the day.

You’ll learn why individual fluid needs vary, how certain medical conditions and medications can affect hydration, and why people with heart or kidney conditions may need specific fluid guidance from their healthcare professional.

Research and Sources:

American Diabetes Association (ADA) — Diabetes management and healthy lifestyle guidance.

National Institutes of Health (NIH) — Research on aging, hydration, and metabolic health.

Mayo Clinic — Dehydration symptoms, causes, and prevention.

Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health — Hydration and its role in overall health.

National Institute on Aging (NIA) — Hydration considerations for older adults.

#seniorhealth  #healthyaging  #over60health  #surgeryrisks  
As we get older, surgery decisions deserve extra care. Some procedures may offer important benefits, but they can also involve serious risks, complications, recovery challenges, and uncertain long-term outcomes. In this 29-minute video, Healing and Health explores five major surgical procedures that older adults should carefully discuss with their healthcare providers before making a decision.

Learn about carotid artery surgery, prostate cancer surgery, abdominal aortic aneurysm repair, knee replacement procedures, and spinal cord stimulator implantation. We explain why age, existing health conditions, surgical risks, expected benefits, and quality of life should all be considered.

Discover important questions to ask your surgeon, why a second medical opinion may be valuable, and how to understand the alternatives before agreeing to an operation. Remember, these procedures can be life-saving or beneficial for some patients. The right decision depends on individual circumstances—not age alone.

Research and References:

NASCET Collaborators — Carotid Endarterectomy in Symptomatic Patients, New England Journal of Medicine (1991).

Wilt et al. — PIVOT Trial: Prostatectomy Versus Observation, New England Journal of Medicine (2012).

Hamdy et al. — ProtecT Trial: Monitoring, Surgery, and Radiotherapy for Prostate Cancer, New England Journal of Medicine (2016).

Greenhalgh et al. — EVAR Trial 1: Endovascular Versus Open Repair of Abdominal Aortic Aneurysms, The Lancet (2004).

Birkmeyer et al. — Hospital Volume and Surgical Mortality in the United States, New England Journal of Medicine (2002).



Subscribe to Healing and Health for more evidence-informed videos about senior health, surgery awareness, healthy aging, and informed medical decisions.

Picture this. You're sitting in a clean
office. Diplomas cover the walls. There
is a calm, confident surgeon across the
desk from you and they look you in the
eye and say, "I think surgery is your
best option." And almost every person in
that chair does the same thing. They
nod. They don't ask what happens if they
say no. They don't ask whether there's
another path. They don't ask how many
times this surgeon has performed this
specific procedure on someone their age
with their health history. They trust
the white coat in the room and they
sign. Now, I want to be honest with you
right away. That trust is often
completely justified. Surgery saves

into their lives better, stronger, freer
from pain because of an operation they
needed. But here is the thing I have
seen over and over that the brochures
and consent forms almost never show you.
For adults over 60, some of the most
commonly recommended surgeries carry
risks that compound dramatically with
age. Risks that are statistically
documented, clinically significant, and
routinely underexplained in a 15-minute
consultation. And in many of these
cases, there are alternatives, real
evidence-based alternatives that nobody
bothered to put on the table. This
channel is dedicated to senior health
education, helping older adults
understand the research behind the
medical decisions they face every day.

five surgeries that are frequently
recommended to people over 60, tell you
the truth about their real risk
profiles, and give you the specific
questions you need to ask before you
ever agree to go under the knife.

thing I share, a simple forward
question, has the potential to change
the entire trajectory of a surgical
conversation and you've probably never
heard it before. Before we move on, drop
your name and your age in the comments.
I'd love to know who I'm talking to
today. Let's begin. Surgery one, coroted
endoctomy.

seniors are told that they have
narrowing in the arteries in their neck,
the coroted arteries, and that this
narrowing puts them at risk for stroke.

this." The operation is called a coroted
endoctomy. The surgeon opens the artery
in your neck, physically removes the
plaque buildup inside the vessel wall,
and closes it back up. In the right
patient, under the right circumstances,
this procedure does exactly what it
promises. It reduces stroke risk. But
here is where it gets complicated. And
this is the part that most people
sitting in those consultations never
hear. The benefit of this surgery
depends almost entirely on whether
you've already had symptoms. This
distinction is everything. If you've had
a transient eskeemic attack, sometimes
called a minstroke involving sudden arm
weakness, slurred speech, or temporary
vision loss that resolved within 24
hours and your curited is more than 70%
blocked. The evidence from a landmark
study called a NASCAT trial strongly
supports surgery published in the New
England Journal of Medicine in 1991.

significant reduction in subsequent
stroke risk for symptomatic patients
with severe stenosis. In that
population, surgery does what it
promises. But what if you haven't had
symptoms? What if a routine ultrasound
just found narrowing and suddenly
there's a surgical recommendation on the
table? Here is where the research
becomes genuinely sobering.
For asymptomatic patients, people who
feel completely fine, the asymptomatic
curited surgery trial known as ACST1
published in the Lancet in 2004 found
that the absolute risk reduction from
surgery while statistically real
requires careful reading. The 5-year
gross reduction in stroke risk was about
5.4 percentage points. But the surgery
itself carries a peroperative cost that
directly offsets that number. The ACST1
trial reported that the peroperative
stroke and death rate in the surgery
group was approximately 3.1%.
And that was across expert centers
participating in a controlled clinical
trial. In routine community hospitals,
published research by Dr. John Burkemeer
and colleagues in the New England
Journal of Medicine demonstrated that
complication rates for curited surgery
climb measurably higher at lower volume
centers. So let me translate that into
plain language. The surgery carries
roughly a 3% risk of causing the very
event it's designed to prevent on the
day of the procedure itself.
When you subtract that peroperative cost
from the gross 5-year benefit, the net
advantage for an asymptomatic patient,
particularly outside of an expert
surgical center, can become very small
indeed. And here is something that has
changed significantly in recent years
that most patients never hear in a
surgical consultation.
Modern non-surgical management of
coroted artery disease has advanced
substantially.
Highintensity statin therapy, optimized

have been shown to meaningfully reduce

batterypowered device implanted into a

reviewing the published literature,

migration, lead fracture, device

requiring replacement, are estimated to
range from 20 to 40% over the devices
lifetime. That range applies to older
generation devices. More modern systems
show lower rates, though long-term data
beyond 3 years remains limited for the
newest technology.
A meaningful percentage of seniors who
receive this device will need at least
one additional procedure to address a
hardware problem. For an elderly body,
every additional surgical procedure adds

already be operating with reduced
capacity. Any implanted foreign object

outcomes.

different responses to the same device.

cancer, not in the low-risk group, most

that consultation happens. Not after,
before. Five minutes of the right

change everything about that
conversation. We've covered five
surgeries.

use this information. Because knowledge

ask does. Before any major surgery, here
are four questions I want you to ask
every single time. Question one, what

that good medicine depends on. I want to
tell you about a patient. I'll call him
Raymond. Raymond was 74 years old,
retired, sharp, the kind of man who
still read the newspaper front to back
every morning and had opinions about all

narrowing in one of his neck arteries.

status, his excellent cardiovascular

optimizing his medical therapy was the
appropriate path for his specific
profile. We adjusted his statin, refined

working on for nearly a decade. He said
something I've thought about many times
since. You didn't give me surgery, you
gave me time, and I used every bit of
it. That is what informed medicine looks
like. Not medicine that reflexively
avoids the operating room. Not medicine
that reflexively runs toward it either.
medicine that stops, asks the right
questions, looks at the whole person,

right for this specific human being at
this specific moment in their life. A
surgical recommendation is not a
verdict. It is not a test of how
seriously you take your health. It is
the beginning of a conversation, and you
have every right to be an active,
questioning, unhurried participant in
that conversation.

room than most patients ever realize.
Use it. Let me bring it all together.
None of this means avoid surgery. It
means be the most informed person in
that consultation room. Ask the hard

not a weakness. Your questions are not
an inconvenience. Your full honest
participation in medical decisions is
not optional. It is essential.
Now, everything I've shared today is
general educational information based on
published medical research and
preventive health principles. It is not
personal medical advice, and it was
never meant to be. Every person's

decision about surgery or treatment,
please have a thorough, direct
conversation with your own doctor or
specialist. They know your history. They
know your body. And that conversation,
informed, unhurried, and honest, is

#bloodpressure  #bloodsugar  #seniorhealth   #hypertension 
Is your blood pressure normal for your age? After 65, the ideal blood pressure target may depend on more than just your age. Your heart health, overall condition, cardiovascular risks, and symptoms can all influence what target is appropriate.

In this 23-minute video, Healing and Health explains systolic and diastolic blood pressure, pulse pressure, morning blood pressure changes, masked hypertension, and orthostatic hypotension. Discover why blood pressure readings at home can sometimes tell a different story from readings taken at the doctor's office.

You'll also learn about important research, including the SPRINT and HYVET trials, blood pressure considerations after 75 and 80, and the connection between blood pressure, stroke risk, and cognitive health. We also explain practical home monitoring habits, how to record your readings, and what questions to discuss with your healthcare professional.

📚 Research & Sources:

HYVET Trial (2008) — The New England Journal of Medicine

SPRINT Trial (2015) — The New England Journal of Medicine

SPRINT Analysis in Adults Aged 75 and Older (2016) — Journal of the American Geriatrics Society

Waldstein et al. (2008) — Pulse Pressure and Cognitive Decline, Hypertension

Trudel et al. (2019) — Masked Hypertension Research, European Journal of Preventive Cardiology


Subscribe to Healing and Health for evidence-based information about blood pressure, heart health, healthy aging, and senior wellness.

 Keywords: 

ideal blood pressure after 65, normal blood pressure for seniors, blood pressure after 70, blood pressure after 75, blood pressure after 80, senior blood pressure targets, healthy blood pressure range, systolic and diastolic pressure, pulse pressure, morning blood pressure surge, masked hypertension, home blood pressure monitoring, orthostatic hypotension, hypertension in older adults, heart health after 65

#throatcare  #silentreflux  #lpr  #acidreflux 
Do you constantly feel mucus stuck in your throat, especially in the morning or at night? Frequent throat clearing, hoarseness, a lump-like sensation, and persistent throat irritation may sometimes be associated with silent reflux (LPR) rather than allergies or a respiratory condition.

In this 22-minute video, Healing and Health explains how laryngopharyngeal reflux, stomach contents, pepsin, and changes in the upper esophageal sphincter may contribute to ongoing throat symptoms. Discover why silent reflux can occur without typical heartburn and why symptoms may become more noticeable as we age.

You'll also learn 7 practical strategies that may help manage reflux-related throat irritation, including better meal timing, hydration, posture, diaphragmatic breathing, identifying food triggers, gentle morning throat care, and elevating the head of your bed.

We also explore common potential triggers, such as coffee, chocolate, citrus fruits, peppermint, spicy foods, fatty meals, alcohol, and carbonated drinks. Remember, triggers can vary from person to person.

If you're over 60 and struggling with stubborn throat mucus, morning hoarseness, or frequent throat clearing, this video will help you understand possible causes and prepare useful questions for your healthcare professional.

📚 Research & References:

Koufman JA — Research on laryngopharyngeal reflux (LPR) and throat symptoms.

Johnston N et al. — Research on pepsin in laryngeal tissue and LPR.

Lechien JR et al. — Research on laryngopharyngeal reflux diagnosis and treatment.

Zalvan CH et al. — Research on dietary approaches to managing LPR symptoms.

Stanford Health Care — Laryngopharyngeal Reflux (LPR) treatment and management guidance.

#eyehealth  #healthyvision  #healthyaging  #seniorhealth  
Can the right fruit help support your eyesight as you age? In this 22-minute video, Healing and Health explores the potential benefits of kiwi for eye health and explains how important nutrients such as vitamin C, lutein, and zeaxanthin support healthy vision.

Discover how antioxidants help protect eye cells, why the macula is important for central vision, and how nutrition may contribute to long-term retinal health. We also discuss the role of healthy fats in absorbing certain nutrients, the connection between blood sugar and eye health, and why people over 50 and 60 should pay attention to regular eye examinations.

Learn practical ways to support your vision through a balanced diet, healthy habits, and proactive eye care. Remember, no single fruit can prevent or cure vision loss, but nutrient-rich foods can be part of a healthy lifestyle.

Research and Sources:

National Eye Institute (NEI) — Age-Related Eye Disease Studies (AREDS).

American Journal of Clinical Nutrition — Research on carotenoids and macular pigment.

Journal of Nutrition — Research on avocado and carotenoid absorption.

Diabetes Care — Research on retinal changes associated with prediabetes.

Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) — Diabetic Eye Disease and Vision Health.


Subscribe to Healing and Health for evidence-informed videos about eye health, nutrition, healthy aging, and wellness after 50.

vision comes from the macula. Here is
what makes the macula extraordinary and
also extraordinarily vulnerable. The
macula contains a unique set of pigments
called macular pigment. These pigments
composed primarily of two compounds
called lutein and zeazanthin function
like a pair of internal sunglasses. They
absorb high energy blue light before it
reaches the most sensitive photo
receptor cells in your eye. They act as
a chemical shield. And here is the
number that should stop you cold.
Studies published in the journal
investigative opthalmology and visual
science have shown that people with
higher macular pigment density have
significantly lower risk of developing
age- related macular degeneration AMD
which is the leading cause of
irreversible vision loss in adults over
50 in the developed world. Not a modest
reduction in risk a significant one. Now
here is the critical piece. Your body
cannot manufacture luteine or zeazanthin
on its own. Not a single molecule. Every
bit of macular pigment you have came
from the food you have eaten across your
lifetime. And as the years go on, if you
are not replenishing it, it thins. Most
Americans are not getting enough. A 2013
National Health and Nutrition
Examination Survey found that the
average American intake of lutein and
zeazanthin is somewhere around 1 to 2
milligs per day. Eye health researchers
generally consider 6 milligs per day of
luteine and 2 milligs of zeazanthin to
be a meaningful protective target.
That is a gap, a quiet, invisible gap
that most people do not know exists
until something goes wrong. So the
question becomes, what fills that gap
most efficiently? What food delivers the
combination of lutein and zeazanthin and
the supporting nutrients the macula
needs in a form the body can actually
absorb that is also realistic for a
regular person to eat regularly? That is
the question the research answers and
the answer is not what most people
expect. Before I tell you the number one
fruit and I am about to I need to tell
you something that most nutrition advice
gets wrong. It is not just about which
nutrients are in a food. It is about
which nutrients your body can actually
get out of it. And this changes
everything about how you evaluate what
you eat for your eyes. The hash shown

excellent. I will come back to that.

when you look at the studies that
specifically measure macular pigment
optical density as an outcome and the
foods that most reliably increase it,
one fruit comes up consistently, kiwi
fruit. Here is why kiwi earns its place
at the top of this list. A study
published in the American Journal of
Clinical Nutrition, a landmark paper
often cited in this field, followed a
group of adults over a 12-week period.
Participants who consume three kiwi
fruits per day showed a meaningful and

the center of their retina. Why does

approximately 0.1 mg per 100 g.

#seniorhealth  #healthyaging  #hygienetips  #over65  
After 65, small changes in personal hygiene can make a big difference in comfort, confidence, and overall well-being. But some common hygiene mistakes may contribute to unwanted body odor without you even noticing it.

In this 14-minute video, Healing and Health explores 9 common hygiene mistakes older adults should be aware of, why body odor can change with age, and simple daily habits that may help you feel fresher and more comfortable.

Discover how aging affects natural body odor, why deodorant alone may not solve the problem, and how to care for often-overlooked areas such as skin folds, feet, scalp, mouth, towels, and pillowcases. You'll also learn practical ways to make bathing safer, improve oral hygiene, keep fabrics fresh, and discuss sensitive hygiene concerns with an older loved one respectfully.

WHAT YOU'LL LEARN:

Why body odor can change after 65

Common hygiene mistakes that may contribute to unwanted odors

How to keep skin folds, feet, and scalp clean and dry

Safer bathing habits to reduce the risk of falls

How dry mouth and oral hygiene can affect breath

When unusual or sudden changes in smell need medical attention

RESEARCH AND SOURCES:

Journal of Investigative Dermatology — Research on 2-Nonenal and Age-Related Body Odor

National Institutes of Health (NIH) — Research on Body Odor and Aging

National Institute of Dental and Craniofacial Research (NIDCR) — Dry Mouth and Oral Health

American Geriatrics Society — Health and Hygiene Considerations for Older Adults

National Institute on Aging (NIA) — Personal Care and Healthy Aging

#nocturia  #nighttimeurination  #seniorhealth  #healthafter60  
Waking up several times during the night to urinate may seem like a normal part of aging, but frequent nighttime urination, also known as nocturia, can have several underlying causes.

In this 21-minute video, Healing and Health explains how aging, changes in ADH (vasopressin), kidney function, blood sugar, circulation, and fluid retention can contribute to nighttime bathroom trips. You’ll also discover how fluid pooling in your legs during the day may return to your bloodstream when you lie down, increasing urine production at night.

Learn about the connection between nocturia and diabetes, kidney problems, heart conditions, prostate issues, sleep apnea, alcohol, and high sodium intake. We also share practical habits that may help reduce nighttime urination, including managing evening fluids, limiting alcohol and excess salt, and elevating your legs before bedtime when appropriate.

Most importantly, understand which symptoms deserve medical attention and when frequent nighttime urination should be discussed with a healthcare professional. Don't automatically assume that waking up to pee is simply part of getting older.

Research and Sources:

National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases (NIDDK) — Nocturia and urinary health information.

U.S. National Library of Medicine (PubMed) — Research on age-related changes in ADH and vasopressin.

Journal of Clinical Investigation — Research on atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP) and kidney fluid regulation.

MSD Manual — Diabetes, glucose, and increased urine production.

American Academy of Sleep Medicine (AASM) — Sleep apnea and its relationship with nighttime urination

Question: How many times do you usually wake up to pee during the night? Share your experience in the comments.

 Keywords:

waking up to pee at night, frequent urination at night, nocturia after 60, nighttime urination in seniors, causes of nocturia, urinating frequently at night, nocturnal polyuria, overactive bladder in older adults, ADH and nighttime urination, diabetes and frequent urination, kidney health after 60, prostate problems and urination, sleep apnea and nocturia, leg swelling and nighttime urination, senior health tips

 Hashtags:

 #frequenturination  #kidneyhealth  #sleepapnea  #healthyaging  #NocturnalPolyuria #diabetesawareness  #prostatehealth  #bladderhealth  #over60health  #seniorwellness

This video is for educational purposes only and does not replace professional medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Persistent or worsening nighttime urination should be evaluated by a qualified healthcare professional.

records.text:
#seniorhealth  #healthyaging  #sleepafter60  #sleeptipsforseniors 
Are you over 70 and struggling to get a good night's sleep? Your bedtime, daily routine, and sleeping environment may all influence how well you rest. In this 22-minute video, Healing and Health explores how sleep patterns change with age and what older adults can do to support healthier, more restful nights.

Discover how your body clock changes after 70, why many seniors naturally feel sleepy earlier in the evening, and how a consistent bedtime routine may improve sleep quality. We also discuss the potential benefits of a regular sleep schedule, the importance of a cool, dark, and quiet bedroom, and common evening habits that can interfere with restful sleep.

Learn practical sleep tips for seniors, including how to manage evening screen time, maintain a relaxing nighttime routine, and create a comfortable sleep environment. Remember, there is no single perfect bedtime for everyone. A bedtime between 9:00 and 10:00 PM may suit some older adults, depending on their wake-up time, lifestyle, and individual sleep needs.

Research and Sources:

National Institute on Aging (NIA) — Sleep and Aging.

Mayo Clinic — Healthy Sleep Habits and Sleep Problems in Older Adults.

Farajnia et al. (2012), Neuroscience & Biobehavioral Reviews — Aging and Circadian Clock Function.

Gooley et al. (2011), Journal of Clinical Endocrinology & Metabolism — Effects of Light Exposure on Melatonin.

Nedergaard et al. (2013), Science — Sleep and the Brain's Waste-Clearance System.

If you are over 70 and regularly experience poor sleep, persistent insomnia, or excessive daytime tiredness, speak with a qualified healthcare professional.

Subscribe to Healing and Health for more evidence-informed videos about senior health, better sleep, healthy aging, and wellness after 60.

and makes returning to sleep harder.
Turn your clock away from view.
If you wake and can't return to sleep
within 20 minutes, get up, sit in dim
light, do something quiet, and return to
bed when sleepiness returns.
Fighting wakefulness while lying in bed
trains your brain to associate bed with
alertness.
Exactly the opposite of what you want.
Let me bring this all together for you.
After the age of 70, your body's master
clock shifts.
Your melatonin rises earlier.
Your biology is asking for a different
schedule, not a worse one, just a
different one.
Fighting that shift is what leaves
millions of older adults exhausted,
foggy, and robbed of the deep sleep
their bodies need most.
The research is clear.
A consistent bedtime between 9:00 and
10:00 p.m. combined with morning light,
a wind-down routine, a cooler bedroom,
and the three evening mistakes we
discussed gives your heart, your brain,
and your metabolism the overnight
recovery window they are biologically
designed to receive.
This isn't about going to bed early
because you're old.
This is about going to bed on time for
the extraordinary complex, still working
body you have right now.
Now, here's what I want to leave you
with.
We talked today about when to sleep, but
there's another question that matters
just as much, and most seniors have
never been told the answer.
What you do in the morning after good
sleep is just as important as the sleep
itself.
The morning habits that lock in your
circadian rhythm, extend the benefits of
deep sleep, and protect your brain
through the rest of the day.
That's what we're covering in the next
video. So, if you don't want to miss it,

That way, you'll be the first to know
when it goes live.
And if this video gave you something
valuable today, please hit the like
button, leave a comment, and share this
with someone you love.
Because better sleep after 70 isn't a
wish, it's a decision, and it can start

#drymouth , #oralhealth , #seniorhealth ,
Do you often wake up with a dry mouth, an unusual taste, or a sticky feeling on your tongue? These symptoms can have several causes, from sleeping with your mouth open and dehydration to medication side effects and certain health conditions. In this 22-minute video, Healing and Health explores the science behind saliva production and why oral health matters for your overall well-being.

Discover how saliva helps protect your teeth, supports swallowing, and contributes to your mouth’s natural defenses. We also explain the role of secretory immunoglobulin A (sIgA), how nitric oxide supports blood vessel function, and how the nervous system regulates salivary glands.

Learn about common dry mouth causes, changes in taste, medication-related symptoms, and why persistent metallic or ammonia-like tastes may sometimes deserve medical attention. 

Research and Sources:

National Institute of Dental and Craniofacial Research (NIDCR) — Dry Mouth Information

American Dental Association (ADA) — Saliva and Oral Health

National Institute on Aging (NIA) — Oral Health and Aging

National Kidney Foundation (NKF) — Kidney Disease Symptoms and Health

MedlinePlus, U.S. National Library of Medicine — Dry Mouth and Medication Side Effects


Subscribe to Healing and Health for more evidence-informed videos about oral health, healthy aging, and the signals your body may be sending.

You open your eyes in the morning and
the very first thing you feel is not
refreshment, not energy, not readiness
for the day ahead.
No. The very first thing you feel is
that your mouth is completely dry. Your
tongue feels like sandpaper. Your lips
are cracked. Your throat feels like you
swallowed a handful of dust while you
were sleeping.
And you immediately reach for a glass of
water because you feel like you have not
had a single drop of liquid in days,
even though you drank water right before
bed.
Now, here's what most people do.
They drink some water, they brush their
teeth, and they completely forget about
it. They think it is normal. They think
everyone wakes up like that. They think
it is just one of those things that
happens when you sleep.
And I am here to tell you today that if
you are waking up with a dry mouth on a
regular basis, your body is screaming at
you. It is sending you a signal.
And if you ignore that signal, you could
be walking straight into some very
serious health problems without even
knowing it.
I am not saying this to scare you.
I am saying this because in over two
decades of medical practice, I have seen
patients come in with complaints that
started as something as simple as a dry
mouth in the morning.
And when we dug deeper, we found things
that shocked them, things they never
expected, things that could have been
caught so much earlier if they had just
paid attention to this one seemingly
harmless symptom.
My name is Dr. Michael Carter and today
I'm going to walk you through exactly
what your body is trying to tell you
when you wake up with a dry mouth.
I'm going to explain the science behind
it, the hidden causes that nobody talks
about, and most importantly, what you
can do about it starting tonight. So,
please stay with me through this entire
video because what I share toward the
end could genuinely change your health
trajectory.
And if you find this information
valuable, do me a favor and hit that
subscribe button and the notification
bell so you never miss these kinds of
important health discussions. Now, let
us start with the basics. Your mouth is
supposed to produce saliva constantly.
Even when you are sleeping, your
salivary glands are supposed to be
working. They slow down a little bit
during sleep. That is true. But they
should not shut down completely. Saliva
is not just water sitting in your mouth.
It is one of the most under appreciated
fluids in your entire body.
Saliva contains enzymes that start
breaking down your food before it even
hits your stomach. It contains
antibacterial compounds that protect
your teeth and gums from infection.
It keeps the pH balance in your mouth
stable so that harmful bacteria cannot
take over.
It lubricates your oral tissues so that
they stay healthy and intact. When your
saliva production drops significantly,
especially during sleep, it creates an
environment in your mouth that is
essentially a breeding ground for
problems.
And the dry mouth you feel in the
morning is a result of that.
But here is where it gets really
important. The dry mouth itself is not
the problem. The dry mouth is the
messenger.
It is your body's way of saying
something deeper is going on and you
need to pay attention.
So, let me take you through the most
common and the most serious reasons why
this might be happening to you.
The first thing I always look at when a
patient tells me they wake up with a dry
mouth is their breathing pattern during
sleep.
And this is by far the most common
cause.
If you are breathing through your mouth
while you sleep, your mouth is going to
dry out. That is just physics. Air is
constantly flowing over your oral
tissues, evaporating the moisture. And
by the time you wake up, your mouth
feels like a desert.
Now, the question is, why are you mouth
breathing in the first place?
Some people do it because of nasal
congestion. Maybe they have allergies.
Maybe they have a deviated septum.
Maybe they have chronic sinusitis.
But some people mouth breathe during
sleep because of something much more
concerning. And that is obstructive
sleep apnoea.
Sleep apnoea is one of those conditions
that millions of people have and do not
even know about.
When you have obstructive sleep apnea,
the tissues in the back of your throat
collapse during sleep and partially or
completely block your airway.
Your body responds by opening your mouth
wider to try to get more air in.
You might snore loudly. You might gasp
or choke during the night.
You might wake up multiple times without
even realizing it. And in the morning,
you wake up with a dry mouth, a
headache, and a feeling of exhaustion
even though you technically slept for 7
or 8 hours.
Now, here is why this matters so much.
Untreated sleep apnea does not just make
you tired. It puts an enormous strain on
your cardiovascular system.
Every time your airway closes and your
oxygen levels drop, your heart has to
work harder.
Your blood pressure spikes. Your body
releases stress hormones.
Over time, this increases your risk of
high blood pressure, heart attack,
stroke, irregular heartbeat, and even
sudden cardiac death.
And it all started with a dry mouth in
the morning that you thought was
nothing.
I had a patient a few years ago, a man
in his early 50s, who came to see me for
something completely unrelated.
During our conversation, I asked him how
he sleeps. And he mentioned that he
always wakes up with a dry mouth and
that his wife complains about his
snoring.
I recommended a sleep study. And sure
enough, he had moderate to severe
obstructive sleep apnea.
His oxygen levels were dropping
dangerously low multiple times every
hour throughout the night.
He had no idea.
He thought he was a good sleeper.
He thought the dry mouth was just
because he did not drink enough water
before bed.
That simple conversation, that one
question about his dry mouth,
potentially saved his life
because we caught it and treated it
before it led to a cardiovascular event.
Now,
the second cause I want to talk about is
one that people really do not like to
hear,
but it is essential that I mention it.
And that is diabetes.
When your blood sugar levels are
consistently elevated, your body tries
to get rid of the excess glucose through
your kidneys.
This means you urinate more frequently,
which is called polyuria.
And when you urinate more, you lose more
fluid, which leads to dehydration.
And one of the earliest and most
noticeable signs of dehydration is a dry
mouth.
If you are waking up with a dry mouth,
and you are also noticing that you are
getting up to use the bathroom multiple
times during the night,
that you are excessively thirsty during
the day,
that you are feeling more fatigued than
usual,
that you have blurry vision or tingling
in your hands and feet,
these could all be signs that your blood
sugar is not where it should be.
Type 2 diabetes develops gradually,
and many people walk around with
elevated blood sugar for years before
they are ever diagnosed.
The dry mouth might be one of the first
clues your body gives you.
And if you catch it early, you can make
lifestyle changes, dietary adjustments,
and if necessary, start medical
treatment that can prevent the
devastating complications of
uncontrolled diabetes.
Things like kidney damage, nerve damage,
vision loss, and poor wound healing.
The third cause is something that
affects an enormous number of people,
and that is medication side effects.
If you take any kind of medication,
whether it is for blood pressure,
depression, anxiety, allergies, pain, or
any number of other conditions, there is
a very good chance that dry mouth is
listed as one of the side effects.
Hundreds of commonly prescribed
medications can reduce saliva
production.
Antihistamines, which people take for
allergies, are some of the worst
offenders.
Antidepressants, particularly the ones
in the SSRI and tricyclic categories,
are known to cause significant dry
mouth.
Blood pressure medications, especially
diuretics, can dehydrate you and reduce
saliva.
Pain medications, muscle relaxants,
anti-anxiety drugs, the list goes on and
on.
Now, I am not telling you to stop taking
your medications. That would be
irresponsible and potentially dangerous.
What I am telling you is that if you
started a new medication and you notice
that your dry mouth got worse, you
should talk to your doctor about it.
There may be alternative medications
that do not have this side effect as
strongly.
Or there may be strategies to manage the
dry mouth so that it does not lead to
further complications.
And speaking of complications, let me
tell you what happens when dry mouth
goes unchecked for a long time.
Because this is something most people
have no idea about.
When your mouth is chronically dry, the
bacteria in your mouth change.
The beneficial bacteria that thrive in a
moist, well-balanced environment start
to die off and the harmful bacteria that
cause cavities, gum disease, and
infections start to flourish.
I have seen patients who had perfect
dental health their entire lives
suddenly develop rampant cavities in
their 40s or 50s.
And when we traced it back, the common
denominator was chronic dry mouth.
Often caused by a medication they
started taking. Gum disease, which is
already incredibly common, gets
dramatically worse when there is not
enough saliva to wash away food
particles and neutralize acids.
And gum disease is not just about your
teeth.
Research has shown strong links between
gum disease and heart disease, between
gum disease and Alzheimer's disease,
between gum disease and diabetes.
So, that dry mouth is not just an
inconvenience. It is a gateway to a
cascade of health problems that extend
far beyond your oral cavity.
The fourth cause I want to discuss is
dehydration. And I know that sounds
obvious, but hear me out because it is
more nuanced than you think.
Most people think they drink enough
water during the day, but the reality is
that a huge percentage of the population
is walking around in a state of mild
chronic dehydration without realizing
it.
If you drink a lot of coffee, tea, or
alcohol, these are all diuretics that
cause your body to excrete more water
than it takes in.
If you exercise regularly and do not
adequately replace the fluids you lose
through sweat, you could be going to bed
in a dehydrated state.
If you eat a diet that is high in sodium
and processed foods, your body needs
more water to process and flush out that
excess sodium.
And if you live in a dry climate or you
sleep with the heater on during winter
or the air conditioner on during summer,
the ambient humidity in your bedroom
could be so low that moisture is
literally being pulled out of your body
while you sleep.
All of these factors can contribute to
you waking up with a dry mouth. And the
solution is not always as simple as just
drinking more water, although that is
certainly part of it.
The fifth cause is one that is becoming
increasingly recognized in the medical
community,
and that is autoimmune conditions,
specifically Sjogren's Syndrome.
Sjogren's Syndrome is an autoimmune
disease where your immune system
mistakenly attacks the glands that
produce moisture in your body, primarily
your salivary glands and your tear
glands.
This leads to chronic dry mouth and dry
eyes, along with fatigue, joint pain,
and a range of other symptoms.
It is more common in women than men, and
it often develops in your 40s or 50s,
although it can occur at any age.
Many people with Sjogren's syndrome go
years without a diagnosis because they
attribute their dry mouth and dry eyes
to aging or other factors.
If you have persistent dry mouth that
does not improve with hydration,
especially if you also have chronically
dry eyes, unexplained fatigue, and joint
discomfort, I would strongly encourage
you to talk to your doctor about being
evaluated for Sjogren's syndrome.
Early diagnosis and management can
significantly improve your quality of
life and help prevent complications like
dental decay, oral infections, and even
lymphoma, which people with Sjogren's
have a slightly increased risk of
developing. Now, let me talk about
something that not many doctors discuss
openly. And that is the connection
between stress, anxiety, and dry mouth.
When you are stressed or anxious, your
body activates the sympathetic nervous
system, which is your fight or flight
response.
This response is designed to prepare
your body for immediate physical action.
So, it redirects blood flow away from
non-essential functions like digestion
and saliva production and toward your
muscles and vital organs.
If you are someone who carries a lot of
stress or anxiety, especially if you go
to bed with racing thoughts and
unresolved worries, your sympathetic
nervous system may remain activated
throughout the night.
This means reduced saliva production,
shallow breathing, mouth breathing, and
you guessed it, waking up with a dry
mouth.
Chronic stress does not just affect your
mouth. It affects your entire body.
It raises cortisol levels, which
promotes weight gain, especially around
the midsection.
It impairs your immune function. It
disrupts your sleep architecture, so
that even if you are sleeping, you are
not getting the restorative deep sleep
your body needs.
It accelerates aging at the cellular
level.
So, when I see a patient with dry mouth
and I ask about their stress levels, and
they tell me they are constantly
overwhelmed, constantly worried,
constantly on edge.
I know that the dry mouth is just one
symptom of a much bigger picture that we
need to address.
Now, let me shift gears and talk about
what you can actually do about this,
because I do not believe in just giving
you problems without solutions. That is
not how I practice medicine, and that is
not how I run this channel. First,
if you suspect that you might have sleep
apnea, please get a sleep study done.
This is not something to put off.
You can talk to your primary care doctor
about getting a referral, or in many
places now, you can even do a home sleep
study.
That is much more convenient.
If sleep apnea is diagnosed, treatments
like CPAP therapy or oral appliances can
be life-changing.
I have had patients tell me that after
starting treatment for sleep apnea, they
felt like they woke up for the first
time in years. Their energy came back,
their mood improved, their blood
pressure came down, and yes, their dry
mouth went away.
Second, address your hydration properly,
and I mean properly, not just chugging
water right before bed, which is going
to make you get up to urinate all night.
Focus on staying well hydrated
throughout the day.
A good goal for most adults is to drink
at least half your body weight in ounces
of water.
So, if you weigh 200 lb, aim for about
100 oz of water spread throughout the
day.
Cut back on caffeine and alcohol,
especially in the evening, and consider
adding a humidifier to your bedroom,
particularly during the winter months or
if you live in a dry area.
Keeping the humidity in your bedroom
between 40% and 60% can make a dramatic
difference in how your mouth feels when
you wake up.
Third, take a close look at your
medications.
Make a list of everything you take,
including over-the-counter supplements,
and discuss it with your doctor or
pharmacist.
Ask specifically about dry mouth as a
side effect and whether there are
alternatives.
Sometimes a simple switch from one blood
pressure medication to another, for
example, can eliminate the dry mouth
entirely without compromising the
effectiveness of your treatment.
Fourth, practice nasal breathing during
sleep.
This might sound strange, but there are
techniques and even products designed to
help you keep your mouth closed while
you sleep.
Mouth taping, which involves placing a
small strip of medical tape over your
lips at night, has become increasingly
popular
and many people report that it
completely resolves their dry mouth.
Now, I want to be clear. Mouth taping is
not appropriate for everyone, especially
if you have untreated sleep apnea or
significant nasal obstruction.
Always talk to your doctor before trying
it. But for many people with simple
mouth breathing habits, it can be
remarkably effective.
Fifth, if stress and anxiety are
contributing to your dry mouth, you need
to address the root cause.
This might mean incorporating a bedtime
relaxation routine, such as deep
breathing exercises, meditation, gentle
stretching, or journaling.
It might mean seeking professional help
from a therapist or counselor.
It might mean reevaluating your
workload, your relationships, or your
lifestyle to reduce the sources of
chronic stress. Whatever it takes,
please do not ignore the role that your
mental and emotional health plays in
your physical symptoms.
They are deeply interconnected.
Sixth,
take care of your oral health
proactively.
If you have chronic dry mouth, you are
at higher risk for cavities and gum
disease, so you need to be extra
diligent. Brush your teeth at least
twice a day with a fluoride toothpaste.
Floss daily.
Use an alcohol-free mouthwash because
alcohol-based mouthwashes will actually
make your dry mouth worse.
Consider using a saliva substitute or an
oral moisturizing gel at night.
Chew sugar-free gum during the day to
stimulate saliva production and see your
dentist regularly, at least every 6
months, so that any problems can be
caught and addressed early.
Seventh, and this is something I feel
very strongly about. Get your blood
sugar checked.
If you have not had your fasting blood
glucose or your hemoglobin A1C tested
recently, please do so.
Especially if you are over the age of
40, if you are overweight, if you have a
family history of diabetes, or if you
have any of the symptoms I mentioned
earlier. Catching prediabetes or early
diabetes can completely change the
course of your health.
With proper diet, exercise, and
sometimes medication, you can bring your
blood sugar back into a healthy range
and prevent the serious complications
that come with uncontrolled diabetes. I
also want to mention something that
people rarely consider, and that is the
role of acid reflux in causing dry
mouth.
Gastroesophageal reflux disease or GERD
can cause stomach acid to travel up into
your esophagus and even into your throat
and mouth while you sleep.
Your body responds to this by reducing
saliva production in some cases, or in
other cases, the acid itself damages the
oral tissues and creates a sensation of
dryness. If you experience heartburn, a
sour taste in your mouth when you wake
up,
a feeling of a lump in your throat or a
chronic cough, especially at night, you
may have GERD that is contributing to
your dry mouth.
Lifestyle modifications, like not eating
within 3 hours of bedtime, elevating the
head of your bed,
avoiding trigger foods, like spicy or
acidic foods, coffee, chocolate, and
alcohol,
and maintaining a healthy weight can all
help manage GERD.
And if those are not enough, there are
effective medications available.
Let me also touch on aging, because as
much as we might not want to hear it,
our bodies change as we get older.
Salivary gland function can decline with
age, And this is a natural part of the
aging process.
However, this natural decline should not
cause severe dry mouth on its own.
If your dry mouth is significant, there
is almost always an additional
contributing factor.
Whether it is medication, a medical
condition, or a lifestyle issue.
So, please do not just accept chronic
dry mouth as something you have to live
with because you are getting older.
There is almost always something that
can be done to improve it.
And here is something that I want to
leave you with because I think it is the
most important point of this entire
video.
Your body is an incredibly intelligent
system.
It is constantly monitoring itself,
constantly adjusting, constantly trying
to maintain balance.
And when something goes wrong, it sends
you signals.
Sometimes those signals are loud and
obvious, like chest pain or difficulty
breathing.
But sometimes those signals are quiet
and subtle, like waking up with a dry
mouth.
The people who live the longest and
healthiest lives are the ones who learn
to listen to those quiet signals.
They are the ones who do not dismiss
small symptoms as nothing.
They are the ones who pay attention to
what their body is trying to tell them
and take action before small problems
become big ones.
So, if you are someone who wakes up
every morning with a dry mouth, please
do not ignore it.
Take it as an invitation to look deeper,
to ask questions, to investigate what
might be going on beneath the surface.
It might be something as simple as your
sleeping position or the humidity level
in your room.
But it might also be something that
needs medical attention.
And the sooner you find out, the better
off you will be.
I hope this video has been helpful and
eye-opening for you.
If it has, please share it with someone
you care about, someone who might be
experiencing the same thing and brushing
it off as nothing.
You might just help them catch something
early that could make a real difference
in their life.
Subscribe to this channel if you have
not already, because I put out content
like this regularly.
Content that is designed to empower you
with knowledge, so that you can take
control of your health.
Hit the like button. Leave a comment
below telling me whether you experience
dry mouth in the morning and what you
think might be causing it.
I read every single comment and I love
hearing from you.
This is Dr. Michael Carter reminding you
that your health is your greatest asset
and no symptom is too small to pay
attention to. Take care of yourself.

#seniorfitness  #ChairSquat #healthyaging  #seniorhealth 
What is one simple exercise that can help adults over 60 build strength, improve mobility, and maintain independence? In this 18-minute video, Healing and Health explores the Chair Squat, a practical strength-building movement that can help older adults improve leg strength, balance, and everyday mobility.

Walking is excellent for cardiovascular health, but it may not provide enough resistance to maintain muscle strength as we age. That is why adding safe strength exercises to your routine can make a meaningful difference.

In this video, you'll discover how chair squats work, how to perform them safely, how they support healthy aging, and how to build a simple exercise routine at home. You'll also learn important safety tips and modifications for beginners and older adults with limited mobility.

Whether you're over 60, 70, or 80, developing stronger legs can help with everyday activities such as standing up, climbing stairs, and maintaining independence. Start slowly, use a stable chair, and choose a level of movement that feels comfortable. If you have joint pain, balance problems, or a medical condition, consult your healthcare professional before starting.

Research and Sources:

Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) — Physical Activity Guidelines for Older Adults.

World Health Organization (WHO) — Guidelines on Physical Activity and Sedentary Behaviour.

National Institute on Aging (NIA) — Exercise and Physical Activity for Older Adults.

American College of Sports Medicine (ACSM) — Resistance Training and Exercise Recommendations.

#hearthealth  #strokeprevention  #healthyaging  #seniorhealth  
Could your nighttime habits be affecting your heart and brain health? As we get older, certain sleep-related health risks deserve more attention. In this 12-minute video, Healing and Health explores five nighttime habits that may increase cardiovascular risks in adults over 50 and 60.

Discover how dehydration, heavy late-night meals, missed medications, uncontrolled nighttime blood pressure, and untreated sleep apnea may affect your health. Learn why sleep apnea matters, how to build healthier bedtime habits, and what steps can help support better heart health and stroke prevention.

Small changes to your evening routine can make a difference. Stay informed, follow your prescribed treatment plan, and speak with your healthcare professional about personal risk factors. Never change medication timing or dosage without medical advice.

Research and Medical Sources:

American Heart Association (AHA) — Sleep and Cardiovascular Health

Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) — Stroke Prevention and Risk Factors

National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI) — Sleep Apnea and Heart Health

American Academy of Sleep Medicine (AASM) — Sleep Disorders and Healthy Sleep

American Stroke Association — Stroke Prevention and Warning Signs


 Keywords:

 nighttime heart attack risk, stroke prevention after 50, heart health after 60, nighttime habits and heart health, sleep and cardiovascular health, dehydration and heart health, sleep apnea risks, late night eating effects, nighttime blood pressure, heart attack prevention, stroke risk factors, healthy bedtime routine, senior health tips, cardiovascular prevention, healthy aging

#seniorhealth  #healthyaging  #seniorskincare  #bathroomsafety  
How often should you shower or bathe after 60? For many older adults, bathing smarter—not necessarily more often—can help protect dry, sensitive skin and reduce bathroom risks. In this 25-minute video, Healing and Health explores seven important facts about bathing, skin health, body odor, and bathroom safety as we age.

Learn why hot water and harsh soaps can worsen dry, itchy skin, what science says about age-related body odor, and why sudden changes in blood pressure during hot bathing may increase safety concerns. 

Discover simple tips for protecting your skin, choosing a comfortable water temperature, using grab bars and non-slip mats, and deciding how often to bathe based on your personal needs. 

📚 Research and Sources

Haze et al. — Journal of Investigative Dermatology (2001): Research on 2-nonenal and age-related body odor.

Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) — Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report (2011): Research on bathroom-related injuries.

Journal of Physiological Anthropology (2022): Review of the benefits and potential risks of Japanese-style bathing.

Environmental Health and Preventive Medicine (2024): Research on blood pressure and body-temperature changes during hot-water bathing in older adults.

U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission (CPSC): Water-heater temperature and scald-prevention guidance.
 

Subscribe to Healing and Health for practical, evidence-informed tips on senior wellness, healthy aging, skin care, and staying safe and independent after 60.

#strokerisk  #sleepapnea  #sleepingposition  #hearthealth  

Could the way you sleep affect your breathing, blood pressure, and heart health? In this 24-minute video, Healing and Health explores six nighttime factors worth understanding, especially for older adults: sleeping with your arms above your head, stomach sleeping, overnight dehydration, sleeping flat on your back, loud snoring, and untreated sleep apnea



📚 RESEARCH AND SOURCES

Circadian Patterns of Stroke — research published in the medical literature.

Morning Cardiovascular Risk and Platelet Activation — clinical research on daily changes in cardiovascular activity.

Neck Position and Vertebral Artery Blood Flow — studies investigating cervical movement and circulation.

Sleep Apnea and Cardiovascular Health — American Academy of Sleep Medicine.

Sleep Position and Brain Waste Clearance — research on sleep and the glymphatic system.

Morning Blood Pressure Surge and Cerebrovascular Risk — research published in Scientific Reports.



Keywords:

 stroke risk, sleep apnea, sleeping position, heart health, senior health, brain health, blood pressure, healthy aging, sleep health, stroke prevention, cardiovascular health, health after 60, overnight breathing, sleep tips for seniors, Healing and Health

Do you wake up several times during the night to use the bathroom? Frequent nighttime urination, also known as nocturia, can interrupt your sleep, leave you feeling tired, and increase the risk of nighttime falls, especially after age 50.

In this 17-minute video, Healing and Health explores how the timing of your daily water intake may help reduce nighttime bathroom trips. Discover the importance of balanced hydration, afternoon fluid intake, caffeine and alcohol timing, sodium consumption, and evening habits that support better bladder health.

Learn how aging affects hormones, kidney function, bladder sensitivity, and fluid retention. We also discuss how prostate enlargement, diabetes, and sleep apnea may contribute to frequent nighttime urination.

You'll discover practical hydration habits, why drinking too little water is not always the answer, and when persistent nighttime urination deserves medical attention.

A practicing urologist with more than 24

Now, in my previous video, I explained

#FecalImpaction #constipation  #seniorhealth  #digestivehealth  
Are you experiencing persistent constipation, abdominal discomfort, or difficulty passing stool? These symptoms may sometimes indicate fecal impaction, a condition in which hardened stool becomes trapped in the rectum or colon. It is particularly important for older adults to recognize the warning signs and understand when medical attention is needed.

In this 23-minute video, Healing and Health explains the common causes of fecal impaction, including chronic constipation, dehydration, reduced mobility, and certain medication side effects. Discover how this condition may affect bladder function, why excessive straining can be dangerous, and which approaches may support better bowel health.

You'll also learn about dietary fiber, proper hydration, sitz baths, suppositories, and the importance of safe constipation management. Most importantly, understand why suspected fecal impaction should be assessed by a healthcare professional rather than treated with repeated home remedies.

Research & References:

American Gastroenterological Association (AGA) — Medical guidance on constipation evaluation and management.

American Society of Colon and Rectal Surgeons (ASCRS) — Clinical guidance on constipation and bowel disorders.

American College of Gastroenterology (ACG) — Clinical information on chronic constipation.

National Institute on Aging (NIA) — Digestive health and constipation in older adults.

Ramkumar D. & Rao S.S. — Efficacy and safety of fiber supplements in the treatment of constipation, American Journal of Gastroenterology (2005).

Important: Severe abdominal pain, vomiting, a swollen abdomen, or inability to pass gas or stool may require urgent medical evaluation. Do not attempt manual removal or use repeated suppositories or enemas without medical guidance.

records.text:
#healthtips  #healthyaging  #seniorhealth  #over80 
What really happens to your body after 80? In this video, Healing and Health explores five important changes associated with aging: muscle loss, changes in sleep and brain health, weaker bones, balance problems, and chronic inflammation.

Discover how protein-rich nutrition, gentle exercise, balance training, quality sleep, and healthy eating may support strength and independence in later life. Whether you're over 80 or caring for an older loved one, these research-based insights can help you better understand healthy aging.

📚 Research Sources:

ESPEN and PROT-AGE Study Group — Clinical Nutrition (2014).

Van Vliet et al. — Gatorade Sports Science Exchange (2018).

Hablitz et al. — Nature Communications (2024).

Walker and Stickgold — Neuron (2017).

Saito and Marumo — Bone health research (2010).

Calder — Biochemical Society Transactions (2017).

Disclaimer: 

This video is for educational purposes only and does not replace professional medical advice. Consult a qualified healthcare professional for individual guidance.

Keywords:

 health after 80, senior health, healthy aging, longevity, muscle loss, brain health, bone health, fall prevention, senior nutrition, elderly wellness, sleep health, chronic inflammation, exercise for seniors, health tips for seniors, Healing and Health
